passage: You want a story, mone? Then your grandpa Joseph will tell you about your Aunt Jaya when she was nine. First week at the new school in Kochi, she walked up to a girl sitting alone at lunch and asked, "Can I share your mat?" By Friday they were a pair. Then came a fight over whose turn it was on the swing, and both of them stomped home. Next morning Jaya went straight to her teacher and said, "We had a fight and I don't know how to fix it. Can you help?" No hiding, no sulking for weeks. The teacher sat them together, and by the end of lunch they were laughing about the swing. That evening Jaya told me, "She wasn't being mean, Pappa. She just wanted a turn too."

qa.q: What did Jaya ask the girl sitting alone at lunch?
qa.a: She asked, "Can I share your mat?"

qa.q: What does Jaya's remark "She just wanted a turn too" suggest about how she thinks about others?
qa.a: It suggests she feels no lasting anger toward her friend; she believes the girl meant no harm, so she can let the quarrel go.

qa.q: What choice did Jaya make the morning after the swing fight, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She went to her teacher and asked for help to fix the fight rather than sulking, which let the friendship recover the same day.

qa.q: How might the girl who had been sitting alone have felt when Jaya came over?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and pleased to be invited, since by Friday the two of them were a pair.

grounding: A grandfather recalls his nine-year-old daughter making a friend, quarrelling, openly asking a teacher for help and assuming her friend meant well.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the museum shelter, and the bus would leave in ten minutes. Uma, ten, had lost the worksheet she and Rafiq were meant to hand in together. "You had it last!" Rafiq snapped. "I didn't mean to," Uma said, cheeks hot. For a second she wanted to hide behind the others. Instead she splashed across to Mrs Pillai. "Ma'am, we lost our sheet. Can we have another one?" Mrs Pillai handed her a spare, damp at the edges. Uma held it out to Rafiq. "Half each? You do the drawings, you're faster." He grinned, and the fight was gone. On the ride back they finished it on their knees, bumping elbows at every pothole.

qa.q: How long did Uma and Rafiq have before the bus left?
qa.a: The bus would leave in ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when Rafiq snapped at her, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and stung; her cheeks went hot and for a second she wanted to hide.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Uma, and why did it work?
qa.a: Instead of hiding, she went to Mrs Pillai and asked for a new sheet, which solved the problem fast and gave her something to share with Rafiq.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt when Uma offered him the drawings?
qa.a: He likely felt included and appreciated, which is why his anger faded and he grinned. 🙂

grounding: Under time pressure in the rain, a ten-year-old asks a teacher for help without hiding and repairs a quarrel with her friend.
